scenes.title: Parameter Store hierarchy as authorization
scenes.visual_overview: This slide explains parameter store hierarchy as authorization by following the pictured security architecture.
visual_walkthrough: Identify the featured AWS service and the full context

The left section organizes configuration into hierarchical paths such as slash prod slash payments and slash dev slash payments. The middle shows a broad GetParametersByPath permission on slash prod; recursive reads can expose descendant parameters that someone expected to isolate by child path. Therefore limit parent-path grants carefully. On the right, SecureString uses KMS encryption, and effective KMS decrypt authorization still matters alongside parameter read permission. Application caches and explicit parameter versions affect the values actually observed by workloads.
Distinguish permission, security and operational responsibilities
A convenient parent-path permission must not become unintended recursive cross-workload access.

scenes.title: Parameter Store tiers and policies
scenes.visual_overview: This slide explains parameter store tiers and policies by following the pictured security architecture.
visual_walkthrough: Identify the featured AWS service and the full context

The left comparison distinguishes Standard and Advanced parameter tiers. Advanced supports larger values, additional supported sharing and policies at extra cost, while API throughput is an independently configured concern. The upper-right policy panel compares Expiration, ExpirationNotification and NoChangeNotification. Expiration can delete a parameter, while notifications report conditions; none automatically rotates the credential in another service. The lower-right lifecycle illustration notes that upgrading from Standard to Advanced is supported but an in-place downgrade is not.
Distinguish permission, security and operational responsibilities
Parameter storage tier, policy notifications and secret rotation solve different problems.

scenes.title: CloudFormation secret references
scenes.visual_overview: This slide explains cloudformation secret references by following the pictured security architecture.
visual_walkthrough: Identify the featured AWS service and the full context

In the left panel, a CloudFormation template uses a Secrets Manager dynamic reference rather than embedding plaintext credentials. On the upper right, a rotated or updated secret does not automatically trigger a stack update or refresh the property in an existing resource. CloudFormation resolves references during relevant stack operations. The lower-right panel adds the consumer lifecycle: environment variables, open connections and application caches may keep older values until an explicit refresh or restart. Secure deployment and ongoing rotation need separate workflows.
Distinguish permission, security and operational responsibilities
Dynamic references reduce credential exposure but are not a rotation or live-refresh engine.

scenes.title: Cross-account Secrets Manager authorization
scenes.visual_overview: This slide explains cross-account secrets manager authorization by following the pictured security architecture.
visual_walkthrough: Identify the featured AWS service and the full context

Trace the three numbered gates. First, the consuming account role must have suitable GetSecretValue IAM permission for the secret ARN. Second, the owning account's Secrets Manager resource policy must authorize that external principal, narrowly scoped. Third, the owner account's customer managed KMS key policy and applicable caller permissions must permit the needed decrypt operation. A valid secret resource policy does not independently grant access to its KMS key. Applicable SCPs, session policies and explicit denies may also matter.
Distinguish permission, security and operational responsibilities
Diagnose caller, secret resource policy and encryption-key permissions separately.
